💬 Parliamentary commission completes review of Hormuz Strait security bill

📌 Tehran, IRNA – The Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission has completed its review of a strategic bill aimed at securing the Strait of Hormuz and ensuring sustainable development in the waterway and the Persian Gulf, the commission’s spokesperson said on Sunday.

Hassan Qashqavi said the commission approved the bill’s remaining provisions, including Article 16, which stipulates that once the law takes effect, the governing regime for the Strait of Hormuz will be subject to the new legislation.
​
Under the approved article, all provisions, laws and regulations concerning the Strait of Hormuz that conflict with the new law will be annulled, Qashqavi said.
​
He added that with the approval of Article 16, the commission had completed its review of the strategic bill.
​
The legislation must still be approved by the full parliament before being submitted to the Guardian Council for final approval.

Inside the CIA’s Darkest Game: When Deep Cover Becomes a Trap


Behind every intelligence operation lies another operation — the one no one is supposed to see. In the shadowy world of espionage, carefully constructed identities can become prisons, bureaucratic rivalries can be as dangerous as enemy agents, and a single mistake can bring an entire mission crashing down.

That world is at the heart of Moscow X, the espionage novel by former CIA analyst David McCloskey. Drawing on his experience inside the agency and at field stations in the Middle East, McCloskey depicts intelligence work not as a seamless machine run by flawless professionals, but as a dangerous system driven by human ambition, secrecy, miscalculations and competing agendas.

The novel follows CIA officers Sia Fox and Max as they pursue a potentially explosive Russian source known by the codename Persephone.

Their target is Anna, the wife of a powerful Russian financier with connections to Vladimir Putin’s inner circle. The operation is built around an elaborate deception designed to make it appear that Russian officials are stealing money — a scheme intended to create suspicion and instability among Moscow’s political elite.

On paper, it looks like a masterstroke of covert warfare. On the ground, nothing is that simple. 

The agents operate through layers of false identities, secret communications and carefully controlled encounters, never knowing exactly who may be watching. Every relationship can become a vulnerability. 

Every conversation can carry a hidden meaning. And every decision made inside the agency can have consequences thousands of miles away.

McCloskey’s CIA is powerful, but it is hardly omnipotent. It is a sprawling bureaucracy populated by people who make mistakes, misread situations and sometimes keep information from their own colleagues. Operations that appear perfectly designed from Washington can become unpredictable once they collide with reality.

That tension gives Moscow X much of its unsettling power.
The most frightening element is not necessarily the enemy intelligence service waiting on the other side. It is the possibility that the machinery designed to protect an operation may itself become a source of danger. Secrecy breeds mistrust. 

Rivalries distort decisions. And the people working under deep cover can find themselves trapped inside identities they created for someone else.

For officers living this way, deception is not simply a professional tool. It becomes a way of life.

McCloskey’s background gives the story an unusual sense of authenticity. Before turning to fiction, he worked as a CIA analyst at Langley and in Middle Eastern field stations. His previous novel, Damascus Station, also drew heavily on the world of intelligence and the experience of officers operating in hostile environments.

But Moscow X goes further into the darker side of the profession. It asks what happens when an intelligence service demands that people spend years constructing elaborate lies — and then expects them to remain psychologically untouched by those lies.

The answer is complicated. Loyalty becomes conditional. Friendships become potential liabilities. Romance can become an operational risk.

Even success may come with a price that cannot be calculated in advance.

And that may be the most disturbing idea at the center of McCloskey’s fictional world: the greatest threat to a covert operation does not always come from an enemy lurking in the shadows. Sometimes it comes from the system itself — from secrecy, bureaucracy and the human beings forced to navigate both.

In the world of Moscow X, the line between controlling the operation and becoming trapped inside it can disappear without warning. And once that happens, there may be no safe way out.

Barron Falls, Australia

Located in Far North Queensland, Barron Falls is a breathtaking natural attraction where the Barron River plunges approximately 850 feet from the Atherton Tablelands down into the Cairns coastal plain. Known as Din Din by the Djabuganydji people, the falls cascade dramatically through the rugged Barron Gorge.

Though much of the river’s flow is diverted for hydroelectric power, the falls are most impressive during the wet season—typically from December to March—when water surges over the cliffs. You can take in the spectacle from multiple vantage points: the Skyrail Rainforest Cableway, the Kuranda Scenic Railway, or the easily accessible Barron Falls Lookout.

⚡️ Reopening of Strait of Hormuz depends on US fulfillment of Iran’s conditions: Araghchi

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, referring to Iran's conditions recently conveyed to the United States in indirect messages through mediators, says Tehran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz provided Washington takes specific actions.

Araghchi told NBC News — in an interview published Sunday — the conditions set out were not new, but were the same that the US had committed itself to, referring to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) that the two countries signed in June but was unilaterally ripped apart by the American leadership.
​
“We want our monies, our assets, which are illegally frozen, to be released. We want to be able to sell our oil,” he told the American broadcaster, saying these demands are matters of right Iran insists be respected.
​
Araghchi said that despite US President Donald Trump’s public comments and rhetoric over the plan relayed to him, the rejection had still not been officially communicated to Iran via mediators.
​
Iran this week offered to reopen the strait and conveyed it to the US through mediator Qatar on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, but Trump said Saturday that he had turned down that proposal.
​
The Foreign Minister, referring to the US president’s rhetoric, clarified that the Islamic Republic remained steadfast in defending itself and firm in responding to any aggression, but has not yet abandoned diplomacy. “It is up to President Trump to choose,” he added.
​
“We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war,” Araghchi told the broadcaster when asked about a US media report that Trump could seek to resume bombing after the midterm elections.
​
“If you ask us, there is no reason why we should go back to diplomacy. I think we shouldn’t miss any chance for peace,” Araghchi said, adding, “We don’t care about U.S. midterm elections, but rather about our national interests.”

The Boulders Beach Penguin Colony is home to more than 2,000 endangered African penguins — one of the only mainland colonies of its kind in the world. Recognizable by their distinctive braying call, these birds were once nicknamed "Jackass penguins."
